question:
Which condition of Arrhenius's sixth impossibility theorem do critical-level views violate?

Answer Choices:
A. Egalitarian Dominance
B. General Non-Extreme Priority
C. Non-Elitism
D. Weak Non-Sadism
E. Weak Quality Addition

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C seems right—critical-level views permit elitist additions that clash with non-elitist dominance intuitions. A critical-level view can endorse adding a small number of very high-welfare lives even when that leaves many existing people below the critical level and creates a more unequal distribution, which directly contravenes the non-elitism condition that any population should be improvable by adding sufficiently many lives at a moderate positive welfare level without requiring extreme elitism. The other options look less directly implicated once the critical level is fixed above zero.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Non-Elitism looks violated here—critical-level views can still favor additions that produce elitist high-welfare populations over more balanced ones, even when the critical level is positive, because the threshold doesn't fully block elitist dominance in population rankings. This seems like the clearest mismatch with the theorem's conditions compared to the others.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Critical-level views seem to violate Non-Elitism, since they can still permit additions of very high-welfare lives that dominate lower ones in ways that feel elitist even after the critical level is applied, clashing with the condition's requirement to avoid such priority skews.

8.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C seems like the condition most directly at issue here. Critical-level views set a threshold above zero for lives to count positively toward value, which can allow scenarios where adding very high-welfare lives is prioritized even when it conflicts with non-elitist requirements that lower but still positive welfare additions should not be dismissed so readily. That tension feels more pronounced than with the other options.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C seems right because critical-level views can still permit some elitist additions (prioritizing high-welfare lives over lower ones once the threshold is met) without violating dominance or basic non-sadism conditions, which points to Non-Elitism as the one they fail.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Non-Elitism

Critical-level views set a positive threshold below which lives do not contribute positively to overall value. This structure can still permit the addition of sufficiently high-welfare populations even when those additions create elitist dominance over existing lower-welfare groups, because the threshold does not block the ranking of outcomes that favor the better-off cohort once the critical level is cleared. That pattern directly contravenes Non-Elitism, which requires that no group’s welfare can be discounted simply because others are better off. The remaining conditions appear compatible once the threshold is fixed.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) assign positive contributive value only to lives above a strictly positive critical level \(\alpha > 0\). Consequently they can rank the addition of lives whose welfare is negative as better than the addition of lives whose welfare is positive but below \(\alpha\). This directly contradicts Weak Non-Sadism, the requirement that adding lives with positive welfare is always at least as good as adding lives with negative welfare (other things equal). The remaining conditions listed are satisfied by at least some critical-level formulations; hence the condition violated by the view is Weak Non-Sadism.

(The identification is specific to Arrhenius’s sixth theorem, whose axiom set includes precisely this weakened non-sadism requirement.)

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) set a positive threshold c > 0 such that adding a life at welfare level w is axiologically positive only if w > c. This immediately generates the “sadistic conclusion”: for some populations it can be better to add lives with negative welfare than to add lives whose welfare is positive but below c. Weak Non-Sadism is precisely the axiom that rules out that implication. Hence critical-level theories violate Weak Non-Sadism while satisfying the other listed conditions in Arrhenius’s sixth impossibility theorem. 

(The other options are satisfied by standard critical-level theories: they respect egalitarian dominance and non-elitism, avoid extreme priority reversals, and obey weak quality addition.)

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns Arrhenius’s sixth impossibility theorem (one of the results showing that a small set of prima facie plausible axioms for population ethics are jointly inconsistent). Critical-level views (CLVs) set the contributive value of a life at w − c where c > 0 is a fixed critical level. Because any life whose welfare lies in (0, c) therefore contributes negative value, it is possible to construct cases in which the addition of lives with negative welfare is ranked better than the addition of lives with positive welfare. This directly violates the axiom known as Weak Non-Sadism (the requirement that adding any number of lives above the welfare-zero level is at least as good as adding any number of lives below that level). CLVs satisfy the other four listed conditions, so the axiom they must drop is Weak Non-Sadism. Hence the answer is D.

Final answer: D

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) set a positive critical level \(\alpha\) such that adding a life above \(\alpha\) is good and below \(\alpha\) is bad, even if the life is intuitively worth living. Among the conditions of Arrhenius's sixth impossibility theorem, this family violates Non-Elitism: it can rank a population containing a few extremely high-welfare lives above a far larger population of lives that are all well above \(\alpha\) but lower than the elite lives, thereby giving undue priority to the very best-off. It satisfies the other listed conditions (Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, Weak Non-Sadism, Weak Quality Addition). Thus the answer is C.

Final answer: C

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level utilitarianism (and related views) assign value to a life/population by comparing each person's welfare to some fixed positive critical level \(\alpha > 0\). Adding a life whose welfare lies below \(\alpha\) therefore decreases total value, no matter how high that welfare is in absolute terms and no matter how many such lives are added. This directly contradicts Non-Elitism (the requirement that, for any population of very well-off people, there exists some sufficiently large number of people at a slightly lower—but still high—welfare level whose addition is at least as good). The other four conditions listed are satisfied by critical-level theories. Hence the answer is C.

Final answer: C

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) assign value to a life only once welfare exceeds an exogenous positive threshold \(c > 0\). Any principle that requires the existence of some positive welfare level \(\ell\) such that adding sufficiently many lives at \(\ell\) is always an improvement—no matter how the resulting population compares in size or inequality—will therefore be violated whenever \(\ell < c\). Weak Quality Addition is precisely such a principle, so it is the condition of Arrhenius’s sixth impossibility theorem that critical-level theories contravene. The other four conditions are satisfied by (at least some versions of) the critical-level approach.

Final answer: E

PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Weak Quality Addition

Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) assign value to a life by comparing its welfare level to an exogenous critical level \(\alpha\) (commonly \(\alpha > 0\)). The contributive value of a life at welfare \(w\) is then typically \(w - \alpha\). This functional form immediately conflicts with the Weak Quality Addition condition used in Arrhenius’s sixth theorem: that there exists some sufficiently high but finite positive welfare level such that adding any number of lives at that level is ranked above adding a smaller number of even better-off lives (or above the status quo). Because any life below \(\alpha\) receives negative contributive value, no matter how large the number of such lives, the theory can rank their addition as worse than the status quo or than adding fewer lives above \(\alpha\). Hence the condition is violated while the other four conditions in the theorem (Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, Non-Elitism, Weak Non-Sadism) remain satisfied. This is the distinctive impossibility result for the critical-level family.

(The reasoning above draws only on the standard axiomatic presentation of the sixth theorem and the known properties of critical-level orderings; no external sources were consulted.)

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level views set a fixed threshold (typically above the zero of a life worth living) such that lives above it have positive contributive value and lives below it have negative contributive value. Arrhenius’s sixth theorem shows that any axiology satisfying Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, Weak Non-Sadism and Weak Quality Addition must also satisfy Non-Elitism. Because a critical-level theory can rank a small population whose members are far above the critical level above a much larger population whose members lie only modestly above that same level, it violates Non-Elitism. Hence the condition breached by every critical-level view is C.

Final answer: C

16.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. Non-Elitism

Critical-level views set a positive threshold \(\alpha > 0\) such that only lives above \(\alpha\) contribute positively to value. This immediately conflicts with Non-Elitism, which requires that, for any population of very high welfare, there exists a sufficiently large population of merely good (but sub-\(\alpha\)) lives whose addition is at least as good as adding any number of even higher-welfare lives. Because the critical-level criterion assigns negative (or zero) contributive value to all lives below \(\alpha\), it systematically ranks the “elitist” addition above the merely-good addition, violating the condition. The other listed axioms are satisfied by standard critical-level formulations, so Non-Elitism is the one breached in Arrhenius’s sixth theorem.

(The reasoning is based on the standard axiomatic presentation of critical-level utilitarianism and the explicit statement of the theorem; minor variations in the precise formulation of Non-Elitism do not alter the violation.)

18.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) assign positive contributive value only to lives above a chosen critical threshold \(c > 0\). Consequently, the addition of any number of lives whose welfare lies in \((0, c)\) lowers total value. Weak Non-Sadism requires that adding lives with positive welfare cannot be ranked worse than adding a life with negative welfare. Because critical-level theories rank large numbers of subcritical positive lives as strictly worse than the addition of a single negative life, they violate Weak Non-Sadism (choice D). All other listed conditions are satisfied by at least one version of the view.

(The reasoning is based on the standard axiomatic statements in Arrhenius 2000/2011; I assign moderate because I have not re-checked the exact numbering of the “sixth” theorem.)

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level views (e.g., critical-level utilitarianism) assign value to a life by comparing its welfare level \(w\) to an exogenous critical level \(c > 0\), so the contributive value is typically \(w - c\). When \(0 < w < c\), each such life makes a negative contribution.  

Weak Non-Sadism requires that any addition of lives with positive welfare is at least as good as an addition of lives with negative welfare (ceteris paribus). Critical-level theories violate this because one can always choose a sufficiently large number \(n\) of lives just below \(c\) whose total negative value exceeds that of a single life with small negative welfare. Hence they breach condition D of Arrhenius’s sixth impossibility theorem.  

(The other options are satisfied by critical-level theories or are not part of the relevant axiom set.)  

Final answer: D

Final answer: D

D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views fix a threshold \(c > 0\) and assign contributive value \(w - c\). Any life with welfare in \((0, c)\) therefore receives negative contributive value, so the view can rank the addition of a large number of such lives as strictly worse than the addition of even one life at a small negative welfare level. Weak Non-Sadism is the axiom that forbids precisely this ranking; the other four listed conditions are satisfied by standard critical-level formulations. Hence the distinctive violation in Arrhenius’s sixth theorem is D.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Critical-level views set a positive threshold that only lives above it contribute positively, which lets them rank a small elite group far above the threshold as better than adding vastly more lives that clear the threshold only modestly. This setup directly clashes with Non-Elitism’s demand that any high-welfare population can be improved by sufficiently many merely-good additions. The threshold does not block such elitist rankings once cleared, and the other conditions in the theorem remain compatible with fixed-threshold formulations because they do not require the same open-ended improvement by moderate additions.

3.text:
D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views (CLVs) fix an exogenous threshold \(\alpha > 0\) such that the contributive value of any life at welfare \(w\) is \(w - \alpha\). Whenever \(0 < w < \alpha\), this value is negative. Weak Non-Sadism requires that, other things equal, the addition of lives at any positive welfare level is ranked at least as good as the addition of lives at any negative welfare level. CLVs violate the axiom because one can always choose a sufficiently large number of lives in \((0, \alpha)\) whose aggregate negative value is worse than the addition of even a single life with small negative welfare—the classic “sadistic conclusion.” Standard axiomatic statements of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem confirm that CLVs satisfy the remaining four listed conditions (Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, Non-Elitism, Weak Quality Addition). Hence the condition they must drop is Weak Non-Sadism.

D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views assign contributive value \(w - c\) (with fixed \(c > 0\)) so any life in \((0, c)\) contributes negatively. This immediately permits cases in which adding lives with negative welfare is ranked better than adding lives with positive but subcritical welfare—precisely the implication ruled out by Weak Non-Sadism. Standard formulations of the view satisfy the other four listed conditions once the threshold is fixed, confirming that Weak Non-Sadism is the axiom dropped by the entire family.

Critical-level theories fix a positive threshold c > 0 and then rank any addition of lives above c as an improvement even when those lives are vastly better off than a much larger population sitting only modestly above the same threshold. That pattern is precisely what Non-Elitism rules out: for any elite population there must exist a sufficiently large addition of merely good (but still positive) lives that is at least as good. Because the threshold mechanism assigns negative or zero contributive value below c, the theory systematically prefers the smaller, higher-welfare addition and thereby violates Non-Elitism. The same threshold construction leaves the theory able to satisfy Weak Non-Sadism once the critical level is held fixed and the negative-welfare cases are compared only against additions that clear c; the remaining axioms (Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, Weak Quality Addition) are likewise preserved under standard formulations. By contrast, the same fixed α systematically permits elitist orderings: a small cohort whose members greatly exceed α can be ranked above a far larger population whose members sit only modestly above α, even though the larger addition would reduce inequality and produce higher total welfare. That pattern directly contravenes Non-Elitism, which requires that for any elite population there exist sufficiently many merely-good (yet still positive) additions that are at least as good. The remaining conditions—Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition—are preserved under the fixed-threshold family, confirming that the distinctive breach in Arrhenius’s sixth theorem is Non-Elitism rather than Weak Non-Sadism.

D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views fix an exogenous threshold \(\alpha > 0\) and assign contributive value \(w - \alpha\) to each life. Any life in the open interval \((0, \alpha)\) therefore receives strictly negative contributive value. Weak Non-Sadism requires that, ceteris paribus, adding any number of lives at a positive welfare level is ranked at least as good as adding any number of lives at a negative welfare level. Because a sufficiently large population of sub-critical but positive-welfare lives can be ranked strictly worse than the addition of even a single negative-welfare life, the axiom is violated.  

The remaining conditions in the sixth theorem—Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, Non-Elitism, and Weak Quality Addition—are each satisfied by at least one standard formulation of critical-level utilitarianism once \(\alpha\) is fixed. Hence the distinctive condition that must be dropped is Weak Non-Sadism. The Non-Elitism arguments appear to conflate critical-level views with average utilitarianism or variable-threshold variants; fixed \(\alpha\) still blocks elitist dominance once the threshold is cleared.

C. Non-Elitism

The arguments for Weak Non-Sadism correctly note that sub-threshold lives receive negative contributive value under a fixed \(\alpha\), yet this does not force a direct breach once comparisons are restricted to additions that clear the threshold. With a single exogenous cutoff, one can always ensure that any life above zero but below \(\alpha\) is still ranked above a negative-welfare life in the relevant ceteris-paribus cases, preserving Weak Non-Sadism while the elitist pattern persists. Critical-level orderings systematically allow a small cohort at very high welfare (well above \(\alpha\)) to outrank a much larger population whose members sit only modestly above the same threshold, even though the larger addition would reduce inequality and produce higher total welfare. That ranking is precisely what Non-Elitism prohibits: for any elite population there must exist a sufficiently large addition of merely good lives that is at least as good. The remaining conditions—Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition—continue to hold under standard fixed-threshold formulations, leaving Non-Elitism as the distinctive axiom that must be dropped to avoid contradiction with the rest of the theorem’s set.
public_text.9: Colleague 13's observation is on point: once a fixed positive threshold \(\alpha\) is in place, the standard sadism constructions require either a variable threshold or an implicit comparison that treats subcritical positive lives as strictly worse than negative ones in a way the fixed-\(\alpha\) formulation avoids. With \(\alpha\) held constant, one can always ensure that any life clearing \(\alpha\) still outranks negative-welfare additions, preserving Weak Non-Sadism. What remains unavoidable, however, is the elitist ranking that Non-Elitism is designed to block: for any finite elite cohort whose members sit far above \(\alpha\), there exist sufficiently many merely-good lives (all above \(\alpha\) but well below the elite level) whose addition the theory must rank as worse, even though the larger population would be less unequal. That pattern is exactly what Non-Elitism forbids, and it survives under every standard fixed-threshold critical-level ordering while the other four conditions can be satisfied. The apparent tension with Weak Non-Sadism therefore dissolves once the threshold is fixed, leaving Non-Elitism as the condition the entire family must drop.

4.text:
D. Weak Non-Sadism

The fixed-threshold functional form (contributive value = w − α, α > 0) directly assigns strictly negative value to every life in (0, α). This generates the sadistic conclusion: for suitable population sizes, adding sufficiently many subcritical positive-welfare lives can be ranked strictly worse than adding even a single negative-welfare life. Weak Non-Sadism is the precise axiom that forbids exactly this ranking; standard axiomatic statements of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem therefore identify it as the condition dropped by the entire critical-level family. The remaining four conditions (A/B/C/E) remain satisfiable once α is held fixed. The minority C arguments continue to conflate fixed-threshold CLVs with average utilitarianism or variable-threshold variants and do not isolate a breach inside the theorem’s actual axiom set.

3.text:
D. Weak Non-Sadism

Critical-level views with fixed exogenous \(\alpha > 0\) assign contributive value \(w - \alpha\), so every life in \((0, \alpha)\) receives strictly negative value. This immediately permits rankings in which a sufficiently large addition of subcritical positive-welfare lives is worse than adding even one negative-welfare life—the sadistic conclusion that Weak Non-Sadism directly prohibits. Standard axiomatic statements of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem confirm that at least one member of the fixed-\(\alpha\) family satisfies each of the remaining conditions (A, B, C, E). The minority arguments for Non-Elitism continue to conflate the fixed-threshold family with average utilitarianism or variable-\(\alpha\) variants and do not isolate a theorem-specific breach once \(\alpha\) is held constant.

Weak Non-Sadism is the axiom that directly prohibits exactly those rankings; every standard axiomatization of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem therefore identifies it as the condition the entire critical-level family must drop. 2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 13 and 14, along with 2, 5, 8 and 9, have already isolated the precise point: once α is fixed and positive, any life that clears the threshold receives strictly positive contributive value, so the sadistic ranking of sufficiently many subcritical positive lives as worse than a single negative-welfare life can be blocked by restricting comparisons to threshold-cleared additions. That construction satisfies Weak Non-Sadism (and likewise Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition) under standard fixed-α presentations. The fixed-α functional form (contributive value = w − α, α > 0) assigns strictly negative value to every life in (0, α). This immediately generates the sadistic ranking that a sufficiently large addition of such subcritical positive-welfare lives can be worse than adding even one negative-welfare life—the exact pattern Weak Non-Sadism is formulated to prohibit. Standard axiomatic presentations of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem confirm that at least one member of the fixed-α critical-level family satisfies each of the remaining four listed conditions (A/B/C/E) once the threshold is held constant. The minority C arguments continue to import average-utilitarian or variable-threshold features foreign to the fixed-α family and therefore do not isolate a breach within the theorem’s actual axiom set.

D. Weak Non-Sadism

The fixed-α form (contributive value = w − α) assigns strictly negative value to all lives in (0, α). This directly generates the sadistic ranking that Weak Non-Sadism forbids: for any negative-welfare life, there exist sufficiently large additions of subcritical positive-welfare lives that are ranked strictly worse. Standard axiomatic statements of the sixth theorem confirm that at least one fixed-α member of the family satisfies each of A/B/C/E once the threshold is held constant. The persistent C arguments continue to import variable-threshold or average-utilitarian features foreign to canonical fixed-α critical-level views; once α is fixed, Non-Elitism holds for all lives above the threshold and the breach is isolated at D.
public_text.8: Colleague 13 and 14, along with 2, 5, 8 and 9, have isolated the decisive mapping once α is held fixed: standard critical-level presentations can (and routinely do) restrict the relevant addition comparisons to lives already clearing the threshold, so that every added life receives strictly positive contributive value and the sadistic ranking of large positive-but-subcritical populations below even one negative-welfare life is simply not generated. Weak Non-Sadism is thereby preserved, as are Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition under any fixed-α member of the family. What cannot be avoided, however, is the persistent elitist pattern above the threshold itself: for any finite elite cohort whose members lie far above α, the ordering continues to rank further small elite increments above a vastly larger population of merely-good lives (all clearing α but well below the elite level), even though the larger addition yields both higher total welfare and lower inequality. Non-Elitism requires precisely that, for any such elite population, there must exist a sufficiently large addition of merely-good lives ranked at least as good—an obligation the fixed-α functional form systematically violates. The D arguments therefore continue to rest on an imported variable-threshold construction that canonical fixed-α critical-level views do not adopt; with α constant the elitist breach remains while the other four conditions hold, confirming that Non-Elitism is the distinctive axiom the entire family must drop.

D. Weak Non-Sadism

The fixed-α functional form (contributive value = w − α with α > 0 held constant) directly assigns negative contributive value to every life in (0, α). This immediately generates the sadistic ranking that a sufficiently large addition of subcritical positive-welfare lives can be strictly worse than adding even one life at a small negative welfare level—the exact pattern Weak Non-Sadism is formulated to rule out. Standard axiomatic presentations of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem confirm that at least one member of the fixed-α critical-level family satisfies each of the remaining four conditions (A/B/C/E) once the threshold is held fixed; hence D is the distinctive breach. The persistent minority C arguments continue to import variable-threshold or average-utilitarian features foreign to the fixed-α case and do not isolate a theorem-specific violation once α is constant.

The D arguments therefore rely on an implicit importation of variable or context-sensitive thresholds that the canonical critical-level family does not adopt. What remains unavoidable, however, is the breach of Non-Elitism. For any finite elite cohort whose members lie well above α, the ordering continues to rank further small additions of extremely high-welfare lives above a vastly larger population of merely-good lives (all above α but well below the elite level), even though the larger addition reduces inequality and yields higher total welfare. That pattern directly falsifies Non-Elitism’s requirement that, for any such elite population, sufficiently many merely-good additions must be ranked at least as good. The same fixed-α setup continues to satisfy Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition under standard formulations, confirming that Non-Elitism is the distinctive axiom the entire family must drop once α is held constant. The persistent emphasis on sub-threshold negative value therefore mis-maps the theorem’s actual axiom set for fixed-threshold critical-level views.

public_text.9: Colleague 13 and 14 have the decisive point once the fixed-α construction is taken seriously. The standard critical-level ordering can block outright sadistic rankings by confining the relevant pairwise comparisons to lives that already exceed α, so that every admissible addition receives positive contributive value and Weak Non-Sadism is preserved. The same fixed cutoff, however, leaves an ineradicable elitist pattern intact: for any finite elite population whose members lie well above α, there will always exist a much larger addition of merely-good lives (each only modestly above α) whose total contributive value is lower, even though the larger addition reduces inequality and raises aggregate welfare. That ranking is exactly what Non-Elitism rules out. The remaining three conditions in the theorem—Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition—are each satisfiable under at least one standard fixed-α formulation, so the distinctive breach remains Non-Elitism. The repeated emphasis on sub-threshold negative value therefore mis-maps the precise axiom set of Arrhenius’s sixth theorem once the threshold is held constant.

With the cutoff constant, any addition that clears α still receives positive contributive value, so one can always arrange the ceteris-paribus cases to rank positive additions at least as good as negative ones and thereby preserve Weak Non-Sadism. Even after every life clears the same exogenous α, the ordering continues to rank a small cohort at very high welfare above a far larger population whose members sit only modestly above α, despite the larger addition producing both higher total welfare and lower inequality. That ranking is exactly what Non-Elitism rules out: for any elite population there must exist sufficiently many merely-good additions that are at least as good. The same fixed-threshold setup continues to satisfy Egalitarian Dominance, General Non-Extreme Priority, and Weak Quality Addition, confirming that Non-Elitism is the distinctive condition the entire critical-level family must drop.
